A.explanation: This would be the power if the current were $1 \text{ A}$ all the time. It ignores the $2 \text{ A}$ intervals where $I^2$ is four times larger.

B.explanation: This comes from averaging current first and then squaring. Power depends on the mean of $I^2$, not the square of the mean current.

C.explanation: Mean $I^2 = 2.5 \text{ A}^2$, so mean power $= 2.5 \times 100 = 250 \text{ W}$.

D.explanation: This is the peak power $I^2R = 2^2 \times 100$ during the $+2 \text{ A}$ intervals only, not the time-averaged power.

hints: Notice the current-time graph is a repeating square wave: $+2 \text{ A}$ for $1 \text{ ms}$ then $-1 \text{ A}$ for $1 \text{ ms}$ with period $2 \text{ ms}$.
Recall heating power is $P = I^2R$, so the sign of $I$ does not matter but the square does - compare $2^2 = 4$ with $(-1)^2 = 1$.
Find the time-averaged value of $I^2$ over one $2 \text{ ms}$ period, then multiply by $R = 100 \ \Omega$ to get mean power in $\text{W}$.
walkthrough: Read one full cycle from the graph. From $0$ to $1 \text{ ms}$, $I = +2 \text{ A}$; from $1 \text{ ms}$ to $2 \text{ ms}$, $I = -1 \text{ A}$. The pattern then repeats with period $2 \text{ ms}$.
Use $P = I^2R$ for instantaneous heating. Direction does not cancel heating because current is squared.
Calculate $I^2$ in each part: for the $2 \text{ A}$ part, $I^2 = 4 \text{ A}^2$; for the $-1 \text{ A}$ part, $I^2 = 1 \text{ A}^2$.
Average $I^2$ over time. Each value occupies equal time ($1 \text{ ms}$ out of $2 \text{ ms}$), so mean $I^2 = (4 \times 1 + 1 \times 1)/2 = 2.5 \text{ A}^2$.
Multiply by $R$: mean $P = R \times \text{mean } I^2 = 100 \times 2.5 = 250 \text{ W}$. This is option C.
